articles.title: THE BELIEVER’S RESOURCES IN THE HOLY SPIRIT
articles.author: E. E. Hoyte

paragraphs.text: I have in mind to call attention to the great resources we have as possessing the Holy Spirit.

We referred today to God’s answer to Moses when, in view of his death, he asked God to set a man over His people who would go out and come in before them. The word was, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit”, Numbers 27: 18. I think the emphasis on the Spirit indicates the pattern or kind of man God had in mind to take the place of His servant Moses, and we may be sure it is also indicative of the unique place the Spirit is intended to have in our dispensation, which we are told is “in faith”(1 Timothy 1: 4)—faith in God and in the Man who has been exalted to God’s right hand. It was as the result of that exaltation that the Spirit was sent down, as it says, “Having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this which ye behold and hear”, Acts 2: 33. The dispensation was set on by Christ; having accomplished the will and counsel of God here in manhood, He was received up into the Father’s presence, and as a consequence the Spirit was sent from the Father in Christ’s name to take up His abode here, completing, you may say, the inauguration of the dispensation. How vast has been the service of these two divine Persons in effecting this, and what a distinctive place They are worthy of in our affections!
In John 7 the Lord is anticipating the descent of the Spirit. In chapter 16 He says, “When he is come”; but here it says, “The Spirit was not yet, because Jesus had not yet been glorified”.

In verse 37 it says, “In the last, the great day of the feast. Jesus stood and cried saying, If any one thirst, let him come to me and drink. He that believes on me, as the scripture has said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water”. No doubt what is alluded to here is the feast of tabernacles which was proceeding, at which the Lord was present. According to Leviticus 23 this feast was the peak of all the yearly feasts commanded by God, being celebrated at the time of harvest ingathering.

At this time they were to dwell in booths amidst cut-down palm branches, willows, and other boughs of trees, rejoicing before God for seven days, love permeating their hearts for God and for one another. The sentiments that were to pervade the occasion are expressed by David in Psalm 133, “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!”, ending with “For there hath Jehovah commanded the blessing, life for evermore”.

The last day, the great day, would be the highest point in their festivity. It was at that time Jesus stood and cried, “If any one thirst, let him come to me and drink”, which would imply that, though experiencing their highest degree of enjoyment, there was something lacking, something more to be desired. “Let him come to me”—think of the effect this appeal should have stirred in their hearts! The Lord was calling attention to the glory of His Person—as the One who superseded the best that Judaism afforded. It was christianity He had in mind. The woman in John 4 left her water-pot at the well, showing that she drank morally and went away filled. Christ was in her; “Is not he the Christ?”, she said to the men in the city. John 4 refers to what springs up in the believer; chapter 7 is what flows out from within—an additional thought—“out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water”. John explains the meaning, “But this he said concerning the Spirit, which they that believed on him were about to receive; for the Spirit was not yet, because Jesus had not yet been glorified”.

We were speaking earlier about the smiting of the rock in Exodus 17—Christ typically had to be smitten for us to get the Spirit. Smiting is a severe thing—“Smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered”, Zechariah.13: 7. Both these scriptures imply that Jesus had to die, but the point in John 7 is that not only was His death necessary, but also His resurrection and ascension and exaltation were a necessity. The great stoop in death had to be taken before His exaltation, as Philippians 2 shows. How it should affect and sober us that our Lord Jesus had to bear the judgment, the wrath of God was poured out upon Him, before we could receive the Holy Spirit. How this should touch our hearts! Christianity is a hallowed thing, based on sacrifice, the sacrifice of the One who offered Himself without spot to God.

Referring to Acts 2, it is good to take a look backward to see what characterised christianity at the beginning. What that word has become today as used in the world is a matter to be deplored. The enemy has got in and spoiled the name publicly, but thank God the Holy Spirit, from an exalted and glorified Christ, as here sustains, in spite of everything to the contrary, the substantiality of christianity in the souls of God’s people. This chapter records the fact that there were suitable vessels for His reception on His descent, and persons are still receiving Him at the present time. “Do ye remain”, the Lord said before going up, “in the city till ye be clothed with power from on high”, Luke 24: 49. According to Romans the Spirit is power. It is important for the young men to study Romans, which is foundational.

Paul enjoined Timothy as a young man, “Till I come, give thyself to reading” (1 Timothy 4: 13), also “Strive diligently to present thyself approved to God, a workman that has not to be ashamed, cutting in a straight line the word of truth”, 2 Timothy 2: 15. I just pass that on to my younger brethren. I know that the pressure of business affairs and the like consumes a good deal of our time, and rightly so; that is not to be condemned. But if we are to fill out our part intelligently in the assembly it is necessary to devote time to reading the Scriptures and to meditation, because the ‘flowing out’ time comes, as our Lord says in John 2: 8, “Draw out now”. It is a test that involves secret history and appropriation of the Holy Spirit.

To return to this wonderful episode in our chapter, “And when the day of Pentecost was now accomplishing, they were all together in one place. And there came suddenly a sound out of heaven as of a violent impetuous blowing, and filled all the house where they were sitting.

And there appeared to them parted tongues, as of fire, and it sat upon each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak with other tongues as the Spirit gave to them to speak forth”. What a day! It was a public demonstration of John 7, “Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water”. Ponder over these expressions. First, “a violent impetuous blowing”, which is explained in the footnote—‘They heard blowing, as of hard breathing’. Breathing would suggest the presence of a person—in fact, a divine Person; then “impetuous” would denote the haste, you might say, with which He moved to take up His abode in the persons assembled. This violent action caused a stir among the crowd of Jews from many nations present—“The multitude came together and were confounded, because each one heard them speaking in his own dialect. And all were amazed and wondered, saying … We hear them speaking in our own tongues the great things of God”.

Now I want to link the great things of God with the passage in 2 Kings 4. The link is in Elisha’s ministry, representing the dispensation of the Spirit, following upon Elijah, typically Christ, being taken into heaven. The chapter prefigures the immensity of the spiritual wealth available to the believer who receives the Holy Spirit. Paul says, “The love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit which has been given to us”, Romans 5: 5. I think the reception of the Spirit is in a certain sense the starting point of the believer’s enjoyment of the great things of God. In the beginning of our spiritual history, like this widow, we have little apprehension of the wealth we received in the gift of the Spirit; “Things which eye has not seen, and ear not heard, and which have not come into man’s heart, which God has prepared for them that love him, but God has revealed to us by his Spirit; for the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God”, 1 Corinthians 2: 9, 10. Like the widow we all have to learn the value of what we have in the Spirit, which the oil typifies. She related her pathetic case to the prophet, the loss of her husband, with the threat of the creditors takings her sons to be bondmen for the debt, not realising the potential wealth in her pot of oil, “Tell me, what hast thou in the house?”, said Elisha. “Thy handmaid has not anything at all in the house but a pot of oil”, as if to infer that the oil was nothing compared with her great need. “ And he said, Go, borrow for thyself vessels abroad from all thy neighbours, empty vessels; let it not be few; and go in, and shut the door upon thee and upon thy sons, and pour out into all those vessels, and set aside what is full”. She poured out until there was not another vessel more, “and the oil stayed”. What this would mean in our day is the inexhaustible supply the believer has in the gift of the Spirit.

She was a subject woman, not an aggressive type of person, so she returned to Elisha in her simplicity to be told what she should do next. “Go, sell the oil, and pay thy debt, and live thou and thy sons on the rest”. But her action only emphasises the fact that we are dependent upon the Holy Spirit to reveal these heavenly things to us, as it says—“We have received, not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is of God, that we may know the things which have been freely given to us of God”, 1 Corinthians 2: 12. But to get the gain of the Spirit’s service it is necessary to follow the lead given—“Go in, and shut the door upon thee and upon thy sons, and pour out into all those vessels, and set aside what is full”. This is an inward, secret idea which involves the power to exclude every foreign influence that might affect our minds. The Lord’s action in the house of the ruler before raising the dead child (Luke 8: 54) gives a lead. The tumultuous crowd had to be first put out of the house; then He went in and raised the child. May the Lord bless the word to us.

Peter’s word in this section of Scripture would have a bearing upon us at the present time, because we are in the waiting time that he alludes to here, waiting for the coming of the Lord Jesus, waiting for the Lord’s appearing. Surely we all love the appearing, the time when Christ shall be vindicated as to every right that belongs to Him, to God the Father’s glory. We long for that time to come. So the waiting time would be a test to us. Peter is seeking to help us in this passage to make use of the time, that it might not be wasted. It is a time provided by God when there is to be moral growth with each one of us, so that we will be ready when the Lord Jesus comes to claim us for Himself. Think of the delight the Lord will have at that moment when He will present the assembly to Himself without spot or wrinkle or any of such things. How it will delight His own blessed heart! But, thank God, His operations are going on.

God is making use of the waiting time to help us to develop morally. I wonder if we appreciate the feelings of God in this waiting period. What a test it is to go through it! It is a test for us brothers anyway, we can say that; I am sure it is a test for the sisters, because Peter would include us all in this passage. We are all in this time. But think of the feelings of God, that God is making use of it. It speaks of it here—“The Lord does not delay his promise, as some account of delay, but is longsuffering towards you”. Think of the feelings of God in this time, that none should perish. That is the thought of God. He does not want any to perish; does not want anyone to die in his sins; but he “desires that all men should be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth”, 1 Timothy 2: 4. Therefore God is long-suffering. Think of the feelings of God at this time. Can we convey these feelings through our feelings? Do we have feelings for men as we wait for the Lord’s coming? Would we desire anyone not to be available to the Lord Jesus when He comes? Oh I think it would exercise us, what Peter is bringing before us in this section, as to whether we can convey to men the true feelings of God as we wait for the Lord’s coming.

Think of the operations of God in the first creation as He could look upon the scene that He had created, to bring man into, to represent Him here on the earth. It says. God looked upon it and it was good. And then think of God creating man in His own image and likeness, and placing man in this scene. But then we know that sin came in to mar the first order of creation. But God has not given up, He is going on; God has the thought of new creation before Him. Peter has that thought here in this passage, that the present heavens and earth are going to pass away, are going to be dissolved. But God is working, He is working in the hearts of men, that man might be preserved alive; “If any one be in Christ, there is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5: 17), alluding to the personal work of the Lord Jesus in each one of our souls. I think we can see it, the elements of the new man, as we look around. Where you see two or more assembled together, you have the expression of it, the thought of new creation, reconciliation seen expressed in persons who represent God here in testimony and have a link with the Lord Jesus, and are in Him; there is new creation.

So that one just thought that we might be exercised by Peter’s word in this passage that we should not waste the present moment, but accept it as a provision of God. God would wait; it is not that God would not fulfil His promise—the promises of God are assured; the will of God is absolute. When God wills something it will take place. It may take time for it to be seen working, but it will take place. With ourselves we will something and it may or may not take place, according to the power that we have in our links with God; but the word of God is absolute and sure, and the promises of God are sure, and the coming of the new heavens and the new earth is linked with the promises of God which are sure to take place.

The world does not understand this. It baffles the mind of natural man. Think of natural man without Christ waiting at the present time for what? They know not what. But we wait according to the promise of God; we have the surety of God’s word that there will be the new heavens and the new earth wherein dwells righteousness. Everything there will be in line in perfection with the mind and the will of God. We are waiting for that time, but God desires in the interim, in this waiting period, to finish His work with each one of us in order that there might be the moral side, completion, seen in us. Think of God working, you might say differently from the way He worked in the beginning. In the beginning God brought in the sphere first, and then brought man into this sphere that He had created. But in new creation God works first with man, to bring man morally into alignment with His thoughts, and then He brings in the sphere. What a sphere it is!—wherein dwells righteousness; everything there is in accord with the holiness of God and the perfection of God.

So God is working to that end. You can see how the completion of that work will produce what Christ can present to Himself. The Lord is longing for that time, but one just thought that in this passage Peter would exercise us at the present time, as we are found in this period, not to waste it. God is not wasting it; He is working; but we are to allow the work of God to reach finality and completion in our souls that we might be morally all that God would desire of us.

So may we be encouraged through this passage of Scripture in the waiting period. We are tested naturally; God test us, you know, every day. What are our links with God? What are God’s thoughts for today? Are we justifying God in His selection of us? We are left here at this time. Why are we left here at the close of the dispensation? Why has God left me here?

Why has God left each one of us here? I think He desires that there might be the expression of the completion of His work seen in men, in persons, at the close of the dispensation. So while we wait, let us allow the work of God to reach completion and finality with each one of us, that there might be seen publicly expressed the idea of the new man as we merge together as brethren, that as we are here the new man is seen expressed livingly amongst us. May the Lord help us on this line and encourage us that we might not waste the present time, but might allow God to finish His work in our souls, for His name’s sake.

I seek help to encourage our hearts, dear brethren, with the glory of the present time. We have been speaking of the inward side of things today and there is a glory about that, a glory that is going through, and is soon to be displayed. Many things that are working out in the saints today have a glory about them that is unique and very soon will be the admiration of myriads.

These features, such as meekness, humility, long-suffering, and patience, may be despised in the world today, but they are going through. However much may seem to be against them, “the meekness and gentleness of the Christ” (2 Corinthians 10: 1), is going through in persons who will soon be clothed with glory.

Isaiah uses fine words when he gets a touch by the Spirit of heavenly things. He says, “I will beautify the house of my magnificence”, Isaiah.60: 7. I would like all of us, the young ones especially, to get some impression that we are connected with a system of glory. From the outside it may seem to be breakdown. As we read, as we should, church history we see what men have done. We see there has been sorrow, there has been conflict, there has been standing for the truth—all these things have been necessary. But there is also another side which I would like to attract you to—that there is a glory about the present time that is going through.
In Exodus 16 Israel had not long come out of Egypt. They were in a very difficult position.

What could they get in the wilderness? What outlook was there? You may raise these questions yourself, you know, as going into employment. You cannot join this association, you cannot claim support from here, or from another source. What outlook is there? How can we get through? Well. God addresses these people who were just wondering how they would get through. Aaron calls the people together and what happens is that as they turned their view to the wilderness “the glory of Jehovah appeared in the cloud”. Oh that something like that might come into your soul today, beloved! They did not then speak about how they would get through. They did not then wonder how they would manage if they did not have this means of support, or that; “the glory … appeared in the cloud”.

I would appeal to you to come into a position where you can see the glory appear! It is there, you know! You may look at numbers elsewhere, you may look at one thing or another, but I would appeal to you to come into this divinely appointed position where the glory appears.

What a view to have! In type another Man came to fill their gaze; that should have, and could have, stilled their murmurings for ever. They were longing for the kind of things they had in Egypt. God says, I will give you something that is infinitely superior. He gave them the manna. Was there ever a day when the manna failed? I ask you to go through these books of Moses. There were murmurings, there were conflicts, there were divisions, but, except on the sabbath, there was never a morning that the manna was not there to be gathered. Joshua and Caleb certainly gathered it. Two men went through. God established in two men what He would have liked to do with myriads, and the glory sustained them above all the breakdown.
Oh that I could convey some impression of the glory carrying things through at its own level.

Turn your eyes, beloved, turn today! God is coming in like this. Think of His grace and His patience. He hears their murmurings, but He does not come in judicially. He might well have upbraided them for what they had done, but He comes in and He gives them an appearance of the glory. Where did it come from? Did it come from Egypt? It was God’s own thoughts that came in, “The glory of Jehovah appeared in the cloud”. And it did not cease. Time after time, in Exodus especially, the glory comes in to meet the situation. Think of God answering things with His glory; strife and complaint on their part, but what God brought in was the exceeding riches of His grace. The glory in Exodus is the riches of divine grace. It says He heard their murmurings and He comes down to those murmurings with His glory, not with a word of rebuke. God feels these exercises that you have. He feels as you do about not having the friends you used to have. The enemy would cause us to be discouraged, but God eclipses the whole thing with a view of His glory, and the glory that He brought in here was that there was manna on the ground. The prophet prayed that the young man’s eyes might be opened to see what there was for him—the whole mountain filled with horses and chariots (2 Kings 6: 17). Things are not just what you see, beloved. What you see may be true, but it is not all the truth.

The breakdown and the sorrows of the testimony are not everything. God has come in with a display of His glory to quicken your affections and to establish your soul in His grace. That grace will never fail. As I said, whatever morning it was, however difficult the day before may have been, however long the night may have appeared to some of these Israelites wrestling with their sorrow, in the morning there was the manna. What a new start, as it were, Christ here in lowly circumstances. He went with His people. That is a fine word in Acts 13: 18 (A.V.), ‘He suffered their manners’. Despite these complaints that there were among the people, God went along with them. He has done that with us, beloved, He has suffered our manners. How bad they have been!—and the answer to it is a view of His glory, in another Man.

Well, this is the inauguration of a system that Paul speaks about. He says it was introduced with glory, but the system we have come into subsists in glory (2 Corinthians 3: 11). It is not now a glory in a cloud—it is the glory in a Man, the Man Christ Jesus. I like that word in Timothy, “God has been manifested in flesh, has been justified in the Spirit, has appeared to angels, has been preached among the nations … has been received up in glory”, 1 Timothy 3: 16. What an answer to the pathway of Jesus! That is our great Priest, beloved; that is how the system is going through. That is how things are going to be maintained. The system subsists in glory because of the place that Jesus has, because of the kind of Man that sustains the system. That is what comes out in Hebrews. It says He has gone in. He was here, went through those circumstances, and was “received up in glory”. He is enthroned in glory and from that position is maintaining the testimony at its true level. Not only that, He is maintaining us. It speaks in our scripture in Hebrews of “the hope set before us, which we have as anchor of the soul, both secure and firm”. It is a fine thing to have an anchor! What storms and exercises we may have known! Thank God our anchor will hold—it is fixed in Jesus. It says, “both secure and firm”. It has often been said that the anchor is no use in the ship. It is only of use as it is attached to the ship and is fixed in firm ground. So, beloved, our anchor is “both secure and firm”. Assembly sorrows never upset the position in heaven. God is affected by them in His feelings, but it is fine to enter His presence and get beyond your circumstances and mine, however oppressive they may be, to get into God’s presence where things are “both secure and firm”. Beloved, you have a place inside there. It says He has gone in; we can all understand Jesus going in in the right and glory and worth of His own Person, but I often marvel at the rest of that verse. It says, “Jesus is entered as forerunner for us”. It means that if He is there, you have a place there. We will soon be there eternally in that glory, and we shall see His face unveiled; we will contemplate His glories. But in the meantime you have a place in there that belongs to you. I think there is a need for us to accustom ourselves and get to know that there is a place there for us. You will have exercises; there are still sorrows in the path, but they do not overcome us as we have a sense that our true place is there.

In Hebrews 9: 24 we have that Christ has entered “into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God for us”. The Lord said to the disciples, “Rejoice that your names are written in the heavens”, Luke 10: 20. Not rejoice that you have been successful in your service, or that you have a good local meeting, or that you enjoy things, but “that your names are written in the heavens”. Beloved, they can never be obscured. Your place there does not depend on your state, your place in glory does not depend on how good you are. It depends on the One who has gone in as Forerunner for us. Oh blessed be His name that He maintains things when I break down! He maintains the saints before God in their true dignity when they go astray. Let us get a greater sense that everything depends on Him. Some of us have said that all depended on men and that everything has broken down. If it depended on men all would have broken down long ago. But it depends on Christ, the Man who endured, and from this point of view it depends on Him alone. He has gone in. Other priests, as it says, had to change, but He “has the priesthood unchangeable. Whence also he is able to save completely those who approach by him to God”.

Whatever your burden, “He is able to save completely”. That is not only your sins, not only those acts and offences that you have committed, the guilt of the sinner away from God. He is surely able to save you from that. But I think it refers as well to the sorrows of the testimony.

I think it refers to the need for encouragement that there may be. It means He is able to change you. He is able to convert you again. Conversion is just like what we read of in Exodus; they turned away from Egypt. It says “they turned toward the wilderness”. Now conversion is just like that, and we need it so often—we have to turn—turn from our own way of thinking; turn from our habits; turn even from the ideals we may have, turn to see God’s view, to see Christ installed in His own glory. In type, Joshua and Caleb proved that He was “able to save completely”. What exercises these two men must have known! Not a local meeting, but a whole nation against them, saying the very opposite to what they were saying. They proved that “He is able to save completely those who approach by him to God”.

O, beloved, as I have said, it depends on Christ, not on me. What a Man He is as installed there! It says, “Such a high priest became us, holy, harmless, undefiled, separated from sinners, and become higher than the heavens”. It has often been said as to man’s affairs that the office confers something on the man, but here is a Man who has gone into the office and conferred a glory upon the office that it never had before. He has the priesthood unchangeable. What a range of glories He has given to it! He has proved Himself worthy of the office. It is not just an act of power, but He has proved Himself so as to win our hearts, to attract us so that we may trust Him. Well, if it all depends on Him, our joy depends on our trusting in Him. For us to come through, for us to have these features of meekness, it depends on our having our anchor in Him. There is a chain that connects the ship to the anchor, and we are responsible to keep those links clear. We are responsible to enter in. It says, “those who approach”. How often do we approach? How often, alas, we may be content to labour at things ourselves, but let us approach. That is another word that Paul uses, “Let us approach”, Hebrews.10: 22. Let us draw near. Let us turn away from the scene of sorrow to have an impression of a scene of glory.

In Exodus 36 and 37 we find a material that bears the gold, not now a glory that comes in, as it did in Exodus 16, but here we have boards and an ark, both made of acacia wood, and they were overlaid with gold. What was underneath was the acacia wood—these moral features of beauty that God appreciates, and clothes with a glory that is suited to His holy presence—
‘Like Jesus! Grace supreme!
Like Him before Thy face;
Like Him, to know that glory beam
Unhindered, face to face!’

These boards had become like that. You would not see in them the sorrows of the testimony; what was prominent at this time was no longer the ability to endure things, but the fact that here that same feature that endured can sustain glory. Think of the saints taking on glory!

You know, heaven will be all the more interesting a place with the saints in it. It is full of interest indeed as we think that Jesus is there, but think of the saints also being there! Think of the number of saints there will be! What exercises they will have gone through in time. But they will all be seen in glory—all like Christ.

‘All like Thee, for Thy glory like Thee, Lord’. Let us be encouraged that, as the inward features of the truth are enjoyed and displayed by us, God can clothe with His glory that which is so delightful to His eye. As you went in, all around was glory. Whether it be a board standing on the west or the north, or wherever it was, that board was covered with glory.

Well, think of the brethren being covered with glory. The Lord says, “The glory which thou hast given me I have given them”, John 17: 22. Think of Jesus imparting that to suffering saints, to saints who have displayed, in measure, the Man who shines in heaven—acacia wood overlaid with gold.

When we come to the ark it is unique. It was overlaid with pure gold inside and outside. It speaks of Christ, unique as to character and in the glory and worth of His Person. Yet the saints take after His character—the boards are overlaid with gold. Well, beloved, it all makes much of Him. Think of this whole environment; all that is in heaven will be suited to Him.

Everything there will be yielding its own tribute of glory and praise to the God who has done these things. May we be attracted to take it on. May we not think that this suffering time is the whole thing. Let us not think of our exercises as the end in view, but be weaned over to God’s side—to see that He is clothing the saints with glory now. We sing, ‘Where the saints in glory thronging’. Think of heaven being full of persons who have come through—a tribute to His own work. The gold had a certain weight about it that had to be borne, and what bears it suitably is the acacia wood.

Well, may we not be discouraged through the present time but may we be encouraged to turn our face to see what God is doing, what He is doing, not outside of us, but in the saints and with the saints. As I said, it will soon issue in a vessel that will be the wonder of the universe, but we are having part in it now; having part in it in our local companies, in our local exercises, household exercises, and daily personal exercises. We are having part in this kind of wood that is going to bear the gold, and is bearing the gold. May we take it on more, for His pleasure.
When adversity befalls him,
This may lead a man to pray—
Often asking God to heal him
And the trouble take away.
Slow he may be to consider,
Is it chance that’s come his way?
God now seeks his ear to open,
He has something He would say.
Maybe many times He’s spoken
Patiently to reach the ear;
Now His hand may add the pressure
All to bring a man to hear.
He would say to him how Jesus
Came into the world to save
Sinners who all need a Saviour,
One whom God in love so gave.
Not a hope has man without Him,
None has power to save his soul;
Just a living touch by Jesus
Saves the sinner—makes him whole.
Strongest men must find their weakness
When they meet the power of death;
All the pride of man is humbled
When he breathes his final breath
Different far it was with Jesus
When He faced that solemn hour—
Death must yield, and He triumphant
Rises from the grave in power.
Joyful news that death is vanquished,
Man’s last enemy o’erthrown
And the glorious risen Saviour
Shares His victory with His own.
He it is who saves completely
Those who come to God by Him,
Gives the soul to know the Father,
Love divine that ne’er grows dim.
Our first knowledge of the Saviour
Fills the soul with glory bright,
And the more we come to know Him
So expands the wondrous light.
All the way we need the Saviour,
Need to hearken to His voice;
As in Bethany ‘twas Mary
Who had made the better choice.
How much sorrow christians suffer
Failing to ‘abide in Him’;
He can save His own completely
In His love that’s never dim.
‘Mid the tests and ‘mid the pressures
That the pilgrim’s way attend,
Listen to Him—He will keep us
Safe in Him until the end.
(Composed September 1976)

The Lord in taking His place at table with the twelve, according to Luke’s account, “when the hour was come” (Luke 22: 14), indicates the dignity and simplicity of divine order. The Lord would have His own distinctive place thus, the Supper being in view, as He will in the world to come when all is subjected to Him. Then the disciples would have a place of privilege in His kingdom according to His appointment, as He says, “And I appoint unto you, as my Father has appointed unto me, a kingdom, that ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel”, Luke 24: 29, 30. The assembly thus clearly would have precedence over Israel, as Paul says concerning the resurrection—“each in his own rank” (1 Corinthians 15: 23), and its administration is to reflect perfect order and judgment, in contrast to the lawlessness of man.

Our place before God is in Christ. He sees us thus according to that order. The table in Exodus, a type of Christ, had things set in order upon it (Exodus 40: 4). These comprised the vessels and the loaves of shew-bread which were to appear in order according to the divine thought. Outside in the orderings of the tribes according to Numbers there was to be order and a place for each, but inside the tribes were represented in the loaves, suggesting our being sustained by Christ typically as food for God and for the priests. Our service to God should reflect that order so that we are conscious of His pleasure and of our place before Him in Christ.
Kingston, Ont.

THE LESSON OF LOT Lot’s name carries the meaning of what is covered, or concealed. He was a righteous man (2 Peter 2: 7), but he so effectively covered up his inward feelings and convictions that he became part of Sodom. That is what happens to a christian who does not show his true colours—he drops to the level of the world and is in dire danger of becoming part of it. In contrast, Abram, strengthened by the priestly service of Melchisedec, and then immediately faced by the seductive proposal of the king of Sodom (Genesis 14: 21), says boldly, “I have lifted up my hand to Jehovah, the Most High God—possessor of heavens and earth” and he is preserved by his own personal link with God, and by stating it clearly. It is like a believer confessing the name of the Lord Jesus and proving salvation in it.

So far as I see, the instructions of Scripture as to the woman’s attire are so worded as to give the prominent place to what is within, but they imply that there will be correspondence in the outward deportment and dress with what is within. This calls for sensitiveness of moral perception as to what will really accord with the testimony. It is not commendable to make haste to follow every current fashion. We have, more or less, to fall in with what becomes general, but even sober people in the world do not hurry to pick up every new fashion or habit, much less should believers have any desire to do so. If the body were held simply as a vessel in which Christ is to be magnified it would have a very great influence on how we dress, and on all our behaviour.
